text: An engineer uses BEFORE(STATEMENT => 'query_id') in a Time Travel query. What data does this return?

options.A: Data as it existed AFTER the statement completed
options.B: Data as it existed just BEFORE the specified statement completed — the state immediately prior to that statement's changes
options.C: Data from 24 hours before the statement
options.D: The statement's result set

explanation: BEFORE(STATEMENT => id) returns the data state immediately before the specified statement completed. AT(STATEMENT => id) is inclusive of that statement's changes. BEFORE excludes them.

text: An UNDROP TABLE is attempted, but a new table with the same name already exists in the schema. What happens?

options.A: The new table is automatically replaced by the restored table
options.B: UNDROP FAILS — you must RENAME the existing table first, then UNDROP the dropped table
options.C: Both tables coexist with the same name
options.D: The dropped table is restored with a suffix (_restored)

explanation: UNDROP fails if an object with the same name already exists. Solution: rename the existing object first, then UNDROP the previous version. This prevents accidental data loss.

text: A table was dropped and recreated (same name) multiple times. UNDROP TABLE is called. Which version is restored?

options.A: The very first version ever created
options.B: The MOST RECENTLY dropped version — UNDROP always restores the latest drop, not earlier versions
options.C: All versions are restored simultaneously
options.D: A random version

explanation: UNDROP restores the most recently dropped version of an object. To restore earlier versions, you must first undrop the most recent, rename it, then undrop again (which gets the next most recent drop).

text: CREATE TABLE restored CLONE orders AT(OFFSET => -3600). What does this create?

options.A: A clone of the current table
options.B: A clone of the table as it existed 3600 SECONDS (1 hour) ago — combining Time Travel with cloning for point-in-time recovery
options.C: A clone of 3600 rows
options.D: An error — AT cannot be used with CLONE

explanation: CLONE + AT/BEFORE creates a zero-copy clone of the table at a historical point in time. AT(OFFSET => -3600) = 1 hour ago. This is a powerful combination for point-in-time recovery without a full restore.

text: MIN_DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 7 is set at the account level. A table has DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 1. What is the EFFECTIVE retention?

options.A: 1 day (the table's explicit setting)
options.B: 7 days — effective retention = MAX(DATA_RETENTION_TIME, MIN_DATA_RETENTION_TIME). The minimum floor overrides the lower value.
options.C: 8 days (additive)
options.D: 0 days (MIN overrides to zero)

explanation: MIN_DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS sets an account-level floor. Effective retention = MAX(object_setting, min_setting). MAX(1, 7) = 7. The object cannot go below the minimum regardless of its explicit setting.

text: A clone is created of a database with COPY GRANTS. What does COPY GRANTS do?

options.A: Copies all grants from every object in the source to the clone
options.B: Copies grants on the DATABASE itself to the clone — object-level grants inside are preserved automatically by the clone operation
options.C: COPY GRANTS only works for individual tables, not databases
options.D: It copies grants to the PUBLIC role only

explanation: COPY GRANTS on CREATE ... CLONE copies container-level grants (the grants ON the database/schema itself). Object-level grants inside the clone are already preserved automatically during cloning.

text: An external stage is cloned as part of a database clone. What is actually cloned?

options.A: The files stored on the external stage
options.B: Only the METADATA (URL pointer, credentials reference, file format) — NOT the actual external files. The clone points to the same external location.
options.C: Nothing — external stages are excluded from clones
options.D: A copy of all files is created in a new location

explanation: External stages CAN be cloned (unlike internal stages), but only the metadata (URL, storage integration reference, file format) is cloned. The actual files in S3/Azure/GCS are NOT copied — both stage objects point to the same external location.

text: Which TWO operations are supported by Time Travel? (Select TWO)

options.A: Query historical data with SELECT ... AT/BEFORE
options.B: Restore dropped tables with UNDROP
options.C: Restore dropped warehouses with UNDROP
options.D: Modify historical data retroactively

explanation: Time Travel supports: (1) querying historical data via AT/BEFORE clauses, (2) restoring dropped objects via UNDROP, and (3) cloning historical states. It does NOT support modifying historical data, restoring warehouses, or accessing Fail-safe.

text: A replication group is refreshed. What happens to the secondary (replica) during refresh?

options.A: The secondary becomes writable during refresh
options.B: The secondary remains READ-ONLY during refresh — consumers can continue querying while the refresh applies incremental changes
options.C: The secondary goes offline during refresh
options.D: The secondary is dropped and recreated

explanation: Secondary databases remain read-only and queryable during refresh operations. Incremental changes are applied in the background without downtime. Consumers experience no interruption.

text: A failover group is promoted (primary fails, secondary becomes primary). What happens to the original primary?

options.A: It is automatically dropped
options.B: It becomes the new SECONDARY (read-only replica) — roles are swapped, enabling the original to serve as the new failover target
options.C: It remains primary alongside the new primary
options.D: It goes offline permanently until manually reconfigured

explanation: When a secondary is promoted to primary, the original primary becomes the new secondary (read-only). This swap enables bidirectional failover — the system can fail back to the original if needed.

text: A consumer creates a database from a share: CREATE DATABASE shared_db FROM SHARE provider.my_share. What privilege must they grant to allow other roles to query the shared data?

options.A: SELECT on each table individually
options.B: IMPORTED PRIVILEGES on the database — this single grant provides access to ALL objects in the share
options.C: USAGE on the database (same as a regular database)
options.D: OWNERSHIP on the shared database

explanation: For shares without database roles, consumers grant IMPORTED PRIVILEGES on the database FROM SHARE to other roles. This single grant gives access to all shared objects. You cannot grant individual privileges (SELECT, USAGE) on imported databases.

text: A provider shares data from MULTIPLE databases in a single share. Which privilege must be granted on additional databases?

options.A: USAGE on each additional database
options.B: REFERENCE_USAGE on additional databases — this grants read access to objects referenced by secure views in the primary shared database
options.C: SELECT on all tables in additional databases
options.D: IMPORT SHARE on each database

explanation: When a secure view in the shared database references objects from OTHER databases, you grant REFERENCE_USAGE on those additional databases to the share. This is required for multi-database sharing.

text: A provider uses SIMULATED_DATA_SHARING_CONSUMER session parameter before adding consumers to a share. What is this for?

options.A: It creates a test consumer account
options.B: It allows the PROVIDER to validate the share by simulating what a specific consumer would see — testing secure views and row-level filtering before sharing
options.C: It sends test data to the consumer
options.D: It measures consumer query performance

explanation: SIMULATED_DATA_SHARING_CONSUMER lets providers test shares from the consumer's perspective before publishing. Set it to a consumer account name, then query secure views to verify row-level filtering works correctly.

text: A share includes a secure view that uses CURRENT_ACCOUNT() in its WHERE clause. What does this enable?

options.A: Only the provider can query the view
options.B: Each consumer sees only THEIR data — the view filters rows by the querying consumer's account identifier, enabling per-consumer data segmentation from a single share
options.C: The view shows all data to all consumers
options.D: An error — CURRENT_ACCOUNT cannot be used in shared views

explanation: Using CURRENT_ACCOUNT() in a secure view's WHERE clause (comparing against a mapping table) enables per-consumer filtering. Each consumer only sees rows mapped to their account — single share, multiple consumers, different data subsets.

text: Can a consumer create a STREAM on a shared table?

options.A: No — streams cannot be created on shared objects
options.B: Yes — consumers CAN create streams on shared tables and views to track changes made by the provider
options.C: Only with ACCOUNTADMIN role
options.D: Only on shared secure views, not tables

explanation: Consumers can create streams on shared objects (tables, views). This lets consumers track changes the provider makes — new rows, updates, deletes — without polling. Snowflake recommends consumers create their own streams rather than providers sharing streams.

text: A provider shares a secure view. The view references a FUNCTION (UDF) in its definition. Must the UDF also be shared?

options.A: Yes — the UDF must be explicitly added to the share or the view will fail for consumers
options.B: No — UDFs used within secure views are automatically available to consumers through the view without being shared separately
options.C: Only secure UDFs need to be added
options.D: Functions cannot be used in shared views

explanation: UDFs referenced WITHIN a secure view do not need to be shared separately. The consumer accesses them implicitly through the view. Only standalone UDFs that consumers call directly need to be explicitly shared.

text: Dynamic tables can be shared with consumers. What restriction applies?

options.A: Dynamic tables cannot be shared at all
options.B: Dynamic tables CAN be shared — consumers see the data but the defining query is hidden (treated like a secure object)
options.C: Only the definition is shared, not the data
options.D: Dynamic tables can only be shared via Marketplace listings

explanation: Dynamic tables can be included in shares. Consumers can query the data, but the defining SQL query is hidden from them (similar to secure views hiding their definition). The provider controls the refresh schedule.

text: A Marketplace listing uses per-query monetization. How is the consumer charged?

options.A: A flat monthly fee regardless of usage
options.B: Based on the number of queries or rows consumed from the shared data — usage-based billing tracked by Snowflake
options.C: The consumer pays nothing; the provider absorbs all costs
options.D: A one-time purchase price

explanation: Per-query (usage-based) monetization charges consumers based on their actual usage of the shared data. Snowflake tracks consumption and handles billing between provider and consumer.

text: A Marketplace listing includes both data AND a Native App. What is this called?

options.A: A hybrid listing
options.B: A data product — listings can bundle data shares, Native Apps, and services together as a single product offering
options.C: A compound share
options.D: A dual listing (requires two separate listings)

explanation: Marketplace listings are data products that can bundle various components: shared data, Native Apps (code + UI), and Snowflake services. This enables rich product offerings beyond simple data sharing.

text: What is a Data Exchange in Snowflake?

options.A: A public marketplace for all Snowflake customers
options.B: A private, provider-managed group of accounts that can discover and access shared data — like a private marketplace for a defined community
options.C: A file transfer protocol between accounts
options.D: A billing reconciliation tool

explanation: A Data Exchange is a private marketplace managed by a provider for a specific group of accounts (e.g., within an organization or partner network). Unlike the public Marketplace, membership is controlled by the exchange administrator.

text: LISTING_TELEMETRY_DAILY in DATA_SHARING_USAGE tracks what?

options.A: Provider storage costs
options.B: How consumers discover and interact with listings — views, gets (installs), and access patterns for listing activity tracking
options.C: Query performance on shared data
options.D: Consumer warehouse credit usage

explanation: LISTING_TELEMETRY_DAILY tracks listing discovery metrics: how many times listings are viewed, how many times they are installed (gets), and which accounts interact with them. Separate from MONETIZED_USAGE_DAILY (billing data).

text: A share has SHARE_RESTRICTIONS parameter. What does it control?

options.A: Whether consumers can re-share the data (resharing)
options.B: Whether the share can be consumed by Business Critical accounts — SHARE_RESTRICTIONS controls cross-edition sharing policies
options.C: The maximum number of consumers
options.D: Which tables can be added

explanation: SHARE_RESTRICTIONS controls whether a share can be provided to or consumed by Business Critical Edition accounts. By default, Business Critical accounts cannot consume non-BC shares (HIPAA data isolation). OVERRIDE_SHARE_RESTRICTIONS bypasses this.

text: A table is cloned using: CREATE TABLE t2 CLONE t1 AT(TIMESTAMP => some_time). If a child table within a cloned schema has a retention period LESS than the time offset, what happens?

options.A: The clone succeeds and skips that table automatically
options.B: The clone FAILS — unless you add IGNORE TABLES WITH INSUFFICIENT DATA RETENTION to skip tables whose retention is less than the time offset
options.C: The table is cloned without Time Travel data
options.D: The table is included with current data only

explanation: Cloning at a historical point fails if any child table's retention is shorter than the requested offset. IGNORE TABLES WITH INSUFFICIENT DATA RETENTION parameter skips those tables instead of failing the entire operation.

text: Can dynamic tables be cloned?

options.A: No — dynamic tables cannot be cloned under any circumstances
options.B: Yes — dynamic tables CAN be cloned (to other dynamic tables or to regular tables), but clones are suspended and must be resumed
options.C: Only via database-level clone
options.D: Only to regular tables, not to other dynamic tables

explanation: Dynamic tables CAN be cloned. When cloned, they are automatically suspended and must be explicitly resumed. They can be cloned to other dynamic tables (preserving refresh behavior) or to regular tables (static snapshot).

text: Which TWO types of objects can now be shared via Secure Data Sharing? (Select TWO)

options.A: Dynamic tables
options.B: Stored procedures
options.C: Semantic views
options.D: Warehouses

explanation: Snowflake has expanded shareable objects to include: dynamic tables, semantic views, Cortex Search services, and models (in addition to tables, secure views, secure UDFs, and external tables). Stored procedures, warehouses, and stages cannot be shared.

text: A provider adds a new account to an existing share. Does the consumer need to do anything special?

options.A: The consumer must accept an invitation
options.B: The consumer must CREATE DATABASE FROM SHARE to access the shared data — they need to explicitly create the database in their account
options.C: Access is immediate with no consumer action
options.D: The consumer must upgrade their edition

explanation: After a provider adds a consumer account to a share, the consumer must still explicitly CREATE DATABASE FROM SHARE to materialize the shared database in their account. It's not automatic — deliberate action is required.

text: A Native App has application roles defined by the provider. What are application roles?

options.A: Roles that exist only within the provider's account
options.B: Roles defined in the app that consumers GRANT to their own account roles — enabling fine-grained access control over app functionality
options.C: System roles like ACCOUNTADMIN within the app
options.D: Roles that automatically inherit from SYSADMIN

explanation: Application roles are defined by the provider within the Native App. Consumers grant these roles to their own account roles to control which users can access which parts of the app. This enables granular access control.

text: Time Travel queries use the CURRENT table schema even when querying historical data. What does this mean?

options.A: You see the table schema from the historical point
options.B: If a column was ADDED after the historical point, it still appears in results (as NULL). If a column was DROPPED, it no longer appears even in historical queries.
options.C: Schema changes are not reflected
options.D: Historical queries fail if schema has changed

explanation: Time Travel queries use the CURRENT schema definition. New columns added after the historical point appear with NULL values in historical results. Dropped columns disappear even from historical queries. Only the data is historical — the schema is current.

text: What is the DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS limit for transient tables, regardless of edition?

options.A: 0 or 1 day only — transient tables can NEVER have more than 1 day of Time Travel, even on Enterprise Edition
options.B: Up to 90 days on Enterprise
options.C: Up to 30 days
options.D: Always exactly 1 day

explanation: Transient (and temporary) tables are limited to 0 or 1 day of Time Travel regardless of edition. Even on Enterprise Edition (which supports up to 90 days for permanent tables), transient tables cannot exceed 1 day.

text: A provider wants to share data that includes references to objects in a SECOND database. What is required?

options.A: Objects from multiple databases cannot be shared
options.B: Grant REFERENCE_USAGE on the second database to the share — then secure views in the primary shared database can reference objects from both databases
options.C: Both databases must be fully shared
options.D: A separate share is needed for each database

explanation: To share data spanning multiple databases: one database is shared normally (USAGE), additional databases get REFERENCE_USAGE. Secure views in the primary database can then reference objects from the secondary databases.

text: A Reader Account user tries to CREATE STAGE. What happens?

options.A: The stage is created successfully
options.B: The command FAILS — Reader Accounts CANNOT create stages, pipes, or shares
options.C: The stage is created but is read-only
options.D: Only internal stages can be created

explanation: Reader Accounts have restricted functionality. They CAN create: warehouses, databases, schemas, tables, views, users, roles. They CANNOT create: stages, pipes, shares, or access the Marketplace.

text: Can a consumer who receives data via a Marketplace listing re-share that data to a third party?

options.A: Yes — always allowed
options.B: Only if the provider has enabled SHARE_RESTRICTION = FALSE on the listing — resharing must be explicitly permitted by the provider
options.C: Never — Marketplace data cannot be re-shared
options.D: Only via Reader Accounts

explanation: Resharing of Marketplace data requires explicit provider permission. Providers control whether consumers can share received data onward. This protects data providers' commercial interests and usage agreements.

text: A change in DATA_RETENTION_TIME from 10 days to 1 day is made on a table. Data from days 2-10 that is currently in Time Travel — what happens to it?

options.A: It remains in Time Travel indefinitely
options.B: It moves into Fail-safe — data outside the new retention period transitions to Fail-safe via a background process
options.C: It is immediately deleted
options.D: It remains accessible for 10 more days

explanation: Reducing retention causes data outside the new window to move into Fail-safe via a background process. It's not instant — data remains briefly accessible in Time Travel until the background process completes, then transitions to Fail-safe.

text: A share includes a secure view. The provider changes the view's underlying query. Does the consumer see the change immediately?

options.A: No — the consumer must refresh their database
options.B: Yes — the view change is IMMEDIATELY reflected for consumers. No action required from the consumer side.
options.C: Only after 24 hours
options.D: Only if the consumer re-creates the database from share

explanation: All changes to shared objects (including view definitions, new columns, data changes) are immediately reflected for consumers. Shared data is accessed in real-time from the provider — no caching, no refresh needed.

text: SHOW TABLES HISTORY is run in a schema. What additional column appears compared to regular SHOW TABLES?

options.A: TIME_TRAVEL_DAYS
options.B: DROPPED_ON — showing the timestamp when each dropped table was dropped (NULL for active tables)
options.C: FAIL_SAFE_BYTES
options.D: RECOVERY_STATUS

explanation: SHOW ... HISTORY includes a DROPPED_ON column displaying when objects were dropped (NULL for active objects). This lets you see all current AND dropped objects within the Time Travel retention window.

text: A consumer installs a Native App from the Marketplace. The app requires access to the consumer's tables. How does this work?

options.A: The app automatically has access to all consumer data
options.B: The consumer must explicitly GRANT privileges on their objects to the app — Native Apps follow the principle of least privilege
options.C: The provider pre-configures access during publishing
options.D: ACCOUNTADMIN access is given by default

explanation: Native Apps follow least-privilege principles. They cannot access consumer data unless the consumer explicitly grants privileges. The app's setup script may request specific privileges, but the consumer must approve them.

text: An account administrator increases DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS from 1 to 30 on a table. Does this retroactively recover data from 2 days ago?

options.A: Yes — all historical data from within the new retention period becomes available
options.B: No — increasing retention only applies to data modified GOING FORWARD. Data already moved to Fail-safe is NOT recovered.
options.C: Yes, but only with Snowflake Support assistance
options.D: Only if the data is still in Fail-safe

explanation: Increasing retention applies to currently active data and new changes going forward. Data that already moved past the old retention into Fail-safe is NOT magically restored by increasing the setting.

text: How many databases can a consumer create from a single share?

options.A: Unlimited
options.B: ONE — a consumer can only create one database per share
options.C: Up to 5
options.D: One per schema in the share

explanation: A consumer can create exactly ONE database from each share. To provide different data subsets to the same consumer, providers must create multiple shares. The consumer can create one database per share.

text: A listing uses 'Auto-Fulfillment' for cross-region delivery. Who pays for the replication compute and storage?

options.A: The consumer pays all replication costs
options.B: The PROVIDER pays for replication compute and storage required by Auto-Fulfillment to serve consumers in other regions
options.C: Snowflake absorbs replication costs
options.D: Costs are split equally

explanation: Auto-Fulfillment replication costs (compute for refreshing replicas + storage for replicated data) are borne by the PROVIDER. This is the tradeoff for cross-region reach — providers pay more but gain a broader audience.

text: A provider grants SELECT on a table to a share, but does NOT grant USAGE on the schema containing that table. Can consumers query the table?

options.A: Yes — SELECT is sufficient
options.B: No — consumers CANNOT access the table. The share must include USAGE on the database AND USAGE on the schema containing the shared objects.
options.C: Yes, but only with fully qualified names
options.D: The GRANT fails with an error

explanation: Shares require the full privilege chain: USAGE on database + USAGE on schema + SELECT/USAGE on objects. Missing any level blocks consumer access. This mirrors the regular access control hierarchy.
